title: Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The three-line motto of BMS, line by line.
body:
Every BMS meeting ends with the same three lines, and every karyakarta knows them by heart. In the 1950s, when socialism and communism were the fashionable words, this motto was an unconventional idea. Here is what it says.

## Nationalise the Labour

This does not mean the State takes over the worker. It means that **the worker is first and foremost a member of the nation**. Labour is not a separate class with an international identity, but a part of the national family, with a stake in the nation's progress.

## Labourise the Industry

Industry exists because of labour. BMS's idea of *labourisation* is that workers should be treated as co-owners, and not merely as employees, once their labour is fairly valued as a form of capital. This is why BMS speaks about workers' participation in management and in the fruits of production.

## Industrialise the Nation

The third line looks outward. A nation grows when industries grow, when production rises and when work is created. For BMS, trade unionism is not only about wages. It is also about **building**.

## One idea, three directions

Together, the three lines give a cycle: a nationally minded worker, an industry that respects its workers, and a nation that becomes strong through industry. It is the practical form of BMS's wider formula, *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*.

Whether one agrees with every application of it or not, the motto explains why BMS tends to combine firm demands with constructive methods.
